lesson_title: Find the Centre With Two Folds
hook_text: No ruler. No compass point. Two paper folds find the exact centre of any circle — and it's a theorem.
clip_script: Cut a circle out of paper — any circle. Now find its exact centre without measuring anything. Sounds impossible? Watch. Draw a chord, any straight line across the circle, and fold the paper so the chord's two ends land on each other. Look at that crease: it cuts the chord perfectly in half, and it crosses at a perfect right angle — the fold forced both at once. Now here's the magic: that crease also runs dead through the centre of the circle. Every single time. So draw a second chord somewhere else, fold again, and where the two creases cross — that is your centre, found by paper alone. This one fold is secretly three theorems: the perpendicular from the centre bisects a chord; the line from centre to midpoint stands at ninety degrees; and the perpendicular bisector of any chord passes through the centre. Engineers genuinely use this to find the centre of worn circular parts. And in your exams it becomes one triangle: half the chord, the distance, one radius — chord twenty-four, radius thirteen, and Pythagoras hands you five. One fold, three theorems, one triangle. That's the whole first act of circle geometry.
visual_style: A paper circle folding in slow motion with the crease glowing; two creases crossing with a burst at the centre point; the fold morphing into a labelled right triangle — 12, 13, and a highlighted 5.
mood: Wonder with a payoff — a magic trick that turns out to be mathematics.
pacing: Slow, satisfying folds up front, a quick three-theorem reveal, brisk triangle finish.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and turn the fold into exam marks.
